Kelp gull (Larus dominicanus) eggs, which weigh between 84 and 92 grams, are incubated for a period lasting 26 to 28 days. Controlled artificial incubation trials confirm that an optimal temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] yields successful hatching after a mean duration of 27 days [ab = 27 days]. Upon hatching, the precocial chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 63 grams [Wwb = approximately 63 grams], a relatively modest mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment already allocated to the development of the large, yolk-rich egg. The downy young are brooded intensively by both parents during the first few days post-hatching, relying on residual yolk reserves before the onset of regular feeding. Growth is rapid in this coastal species, and the nestlings quickly progress through the early feather-growing stages, doubling their body mass within the first week under optimal conditions.

The development of the juvenile plumage and the attainment of flight capacity mark a critical transition in the life cycle of the Kelp gull. Under the core body temperature typical of active metabolic function in this species, approximately 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], fledging occurs at a mean age of 60 days after hatching [tx = 60 days after hatching]. This prolonged nestling period is characteristic of large gulls and allows for the complete maturation of flight feathers and the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves to support the post-fledging dispersal phase. During this time, the growing juvenile bird is heavily dependent on the provisioning adults, which bring a diet consisting largely of intertidal invertebrates, fish offal, and discarded human food. The fledgling precursor stage is marked by vigorous wing-flapping exercises on the ground near the colony.

Once nutritional independence is achieved, the immature bird enters a lengthy sub-adult phase characterized by progressive plumage changes and continued somatic growth. Estimates for related Larus species in the AnAge database suggest that maximum lifespan under field conditions may reach up to 30 years [am = up to 30 years] in this lineage at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. During these pre-reproductive years, juvenile birds typically disperse widely along coastlines, joining large non-breeding flocks and honing their foraging skills. This extended juvenile period is a common life-history strategy among large gulls, allowing individuals to attain the large adult body size necessary for successful competition at breeding sites. The birds do not begin to show signs of gonadal activity until they have completed several annual molt cycles.

The attainment of sexual maturity in the Kelp gull is a gradual process, with puberty being reached at approximately 180 days after hatching [tp = approximately 180 days after hatching], although behavioral and physiological readiness for breeding typically lags considerably behind this initial maturation at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C] of the gonads. A more reliable indicator of reproductive onset is the age at which individuals first establish a breeding territory and successfully produce a clutch. Adult Kelp gulls exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males routinely attaining a larger ultimate wet weight than females. The maximum adult body mass recorded for males is approximately 1,050 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,050 grams], whereas females typically reach an ultimate wet weight of around 830 grams [Wwi = around 830 grams]. This difference in mass is likely related to the differing roles each sex plays in territorial defense and chick provisioning. The annual reproductive output of a breeding pair is modest; females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = a single clutch per year], containing two to three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = containing two to three eggs per clutch]. This low fecundity is compensated for by high adult survival rates and a long reproductive lifespan, which together allow the species to maintain stable populations across its extensive Southern Hemisphere range.
